topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education context; applicability to workplace AI literacy development may be limited without sector-specific adaptation.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most relevant to your organisation's strategic priorities, then map these to specific roles rather than attempting broad, undifferentiated upskilling.

Consider blended learning approaches (combining theory, hands-on practice, and case studies) rather than standalone workshops, as higher education evidence suggests this improves retention and capability transfer.
Embed AI literacy development into existing professional development pathways and assessment frameworks to increase adoption and demonstrate organisational commitment.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher education context; applicability to organisational AI literacy development in corporate settings requires translation and adaptation.
takeaways: Use a multi-domain framework (technical, critical thinking, ethical, practical application) rather than single-skill training when designing AI literacy programs — this addresses common gaps where employees understand AI concepts but lack critical evaluation or ethical reasoning.

Position AI literacy as a foundational meta-skill that enhances other capabilities, not as standalone training — this shifts the business case from 'learn AI' to 'use AI to do your job better' and improves uptake.

The four-domain model suggests you should audit your current AI training to identify which domains (e.g. ethics, hands-on practice) are missing — most corporate programs lean heavily on technical content while neglecting critical thinking and ethical considerations.

articles.title: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce - U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.snippet: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce  U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes Department of Labor initiatives, grant schemes, and policy that do not apply in Australia. Australian organisations should instead consult local government and industry bodies for comparable AI literacy programs.
takeaways: US government is prioritising AI literacy as a workforce development issue; Australian employers should check equivalent initiatives from state and federal training bodies and industry associations.

Government-backed AI literacy programs suggest emerging policy consensus that basic AI understanding is becoming a baseline work skill — consider how this might inform your organisational capability planning.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher vocational education context; geographic scope unclear from title. Findings on competency ladder design may apply to vocational training but generalisability to workplace professional development in Australia depends on sample characteristics not visible in snippet.
takeaways: Consider structuring AI literacy programmes as progressive competency ladders rather than single-level courses—this scaffolding approach appears validated for learner progression in vocational settings.
Use competency-based assessment frameworks when designing AI skills pathways to ensure learners meet defined benchmarks before advancing, rather than time-based progression alone.

articles.title: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation - Nature
articles.snippet: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone — the geographic scope, sample size, and specific sectors studied are not indicated in the provided information.
takeaways: Employability skills (beyond technical AI knowledge) are a critical lever for securing quality employment in AI-transformed labour markets — organisations should prioritise upskilling programmes that build adaptability, communication, and problem-solving alongside AI literacy.

Academic achievement and motivation function as mediating factors in how employability skills translate to job quality — screening for and supporting intrinsic motivation in learners may amplify the ROI of AI capability-building programmes.

AI-driven labour market shifts create new quality-of-employment risks; design AI literacy interventions to explicitly build the soft skills and resilience that protect workers from displacement or underemployment, not just technical competence.

articles.title: New AI Course from DOL Targets Broad Workforce Readiness - SHRM
articles.snippet: New AI Course from DOL Targets Broad Workforce Readiness  SHRM
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes a US Department of Labor (DOL) initiative and training program that would not directly apply to Australian organisations, though the general approach to AI literacy could be adapted.
takeaways: US-specific: The DOL's AI course model shows how government-led workforce development can address AI literacy gaps at scale, but Australian organisations should consult local training frameworks and government initiatives rather than relying on US DOL programs.
Consider whether your organisation needs a broad, foundational AI literacy program similar to DOL's approach, or targeted upskilling for specific roles — timing and scope matter for engagement.
Government-backed training programs can legitimise AI learning as essential rather than optional; explore whether your industry or state has equivalent initiatives you can leverage or partner with.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings on AI's effect on job insecurity are relevant across sectors, but the study's geographic scope is unclear, and generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Build employee self-efficacy around AI tools through targeted training and skill-building programs; staff with higher self-efficacy experience lower job insecurity when AI is introduced.

Leaders should adopt transformational leadership behaviours (vision-setting, individualised support, intellectual stimulation) during AI implementation to buffer against employee anxiety about job displacement.

When rolling out AI in your team, address job insecurity proactively by strengthening both individual capability and leadership presence — these factors can meaningfully reduce negative psychological impacts.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in certain cultural settings (notably East Asian organisations). Findings may not transfer directly to egalitarian or distributed leadership models common in many Western organisations.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools by involving employees in customising and adapting AI systems to their workflows — this strengthens collaboration and reduces resistance to AI adoption.

In hierarchical or paternalistic organisational cultures, leaders should actively guide and legitimise AI crafting practices, as employee autonomy in shaping AI tools is more effective when endorsed from above.

AI crafting (customisation and configuration of AI systems) acts as a mechanism through which ownership translates into collaborative behaviour — invest in enabling employees to modify AI tools rather than imposing rigid implementations.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not evident from the title and snippet alone. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) is likely applicable across contexts, but findings may vary by sector, organization size, and AI implementation maturity.
takeaways: Monitor how employees respond to AI adoption—some may proactively reshape their roles (approach) while others withdraw or resist (avoidance). Design implementation strategies that encourage approach behaviors through clear communication about role evolution.

Job crafting (how employees modify their tasks and relationships) is a key psychological response to AI adoption. Managers should create space for employees to actively shape their roles rather than passively accepting changes.

Use approach-avoidance theory to segment your workforce during AI rollout—identify early adopters versus anxious employees and tailor support (training, mentoring, involvement in design) to reduce avoidance behaviors and maximize constructive adaptation.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — the title suggests a theoretical or empirical study of psychological pathways, but sample composition, size, and geographic scope cannot be determined from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Design employee-AI collaboration frameworks that activate both psychological pathways to engagement — likely competence/mastery (through meaningful task allocation to AI) and autonomy/control (through user agency in how AI is deployed) — rather than treating AI as a replacement tool.

Assess current AI implementations in your organisation for whether they enhance or diminish employee sense of control and skill development; misaligned deployments may suppress engagement even if efficiency gains are realised.

articles.title: When resilience backfires: the counterintuitive effect of employee resilience in high-tech surveillance environments - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When resilience backfires: the counterintuitive effect of employee resilience in high-tech surveillance environments  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — appears to examine surveillance environments but geographic scope and sector breadth are not detailed. Findings may be particularly relevant to high-tech and monitoring-intensive roles but applicability across other industries and geographies requires the full article.
takeaways: High resilience in surveillance-heavy environments may paradoxically reduce employees' willingness to voice concerns or push back against monitoring practices, potentially enabling problematic workplace cultures — consider balancing resilience training with psychological safety initiatives that actively encourage questioning.

When implementing monitoring technologies, assess whether your organisation is inadvertently selecting for or reinforcing overly compliant employees who absorb stress rather than address systemic issues; create explicit channels for feedback on surveillance practices themselves.

Resilience-building programs should be paired with organisational accountability measures; resilience alone without transparency and fairness in surveillance policies may mask underlying problems rather than solve them.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — snippet does not specify sample size, geography, sector, or methodology. Full article needed to assess how findings might apply across different organisational contexts and regions.
takeaways: Prioritise psychological safety initiatives as a core intervention when implementing AI tools — workers who feel safe to voice concerns, ask questions, and admit mistakes about AI are less likely to experience depression-related outcomes.

When rolling out AI adoption, explicitly address worker anxiety by creating forums for feedback, transparent communication about AI's role and limitations, and clear channels for workers to report concerns without fear of retaliation.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data, geographic scope, or sector focus. Likely reflects US business school viewpoint and may not account for Australian labour market, regulations, or workplace norms.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most vulnerable to AI displacement and proactively design reskilling pathways before disruption occurs, rather than reacting to workforce changes.
Use AI adoption as a catalyst to reshape job design — focus teams on high-value human work (creativity, relationship-building, complex problem-solving) and offload routine tasks to AI systems.

Engage employees early in AI implementation conversations to understand their concerns about job security; transparent communication about how AI will augment rather than replace roles can reduce resistance and support behaviour change.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology — the title suggests a theoretical or empirical framework but the snippet does not indicate sample size, geographic scope, or sector specificity.
takeaways: Design AI systems with explicit attention to inclusive outcomes by pairing algorithmic work design with active DEI interventions — passive diversity statements are insufficient to prevent algorithmic bias.
Cultivate a diversity-supportive organisational culture before or alongside AI implementation; this culture acts as a buffer that helps teams identify and challenge algorithmically-driven inequities.

Audit how AI-driven workflows assign tasks and opportunities to ensure they don't inadvertently disadvantage underrepresented groups — algorithmic fairness requires ongoing human oversight, not one-time configuration.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on global client experience and may reflect practices in large multinational organisations, but specific data sources and sample composition are not evident from the snippet.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology rollout — this shifts focus from implementation timelines to employee readiness, mindset, and skill development.

Design change management interventions that address the psychological and organisational barriers to AI adoption alongside technical training, since resistance often stems from uncertainty about roles and job security.
Prioritise early identification and upskilling of AI champions within teams to model adoption behaviours and reduce peer anxiety about AI tools.

articles.title: AI-induced job crafting: a systematic review of cognitive appraisal pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI-induced job crafting: a systematic review of cognitive appraisal pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on included studies' geographic spread and sector representation, which are not detailed in the snippet. Systematic reviews of job crafting research typically draw from diverse global samples, but limitations depend on the primary studies reviewed.
takeaways: Employees who experience AI integration at work can be supported to reframe their role proactively through job crafting—redesigning tasks, relationships, or meaning—rather than passively accepting disruption; understanding cognitive appraisal pathways helps managers identify which reframing strategies will resonate.

Cognitive appraisal of AI (threat vs. opportunity) is a key lever: organisations can shift employee mindset from threat-focused ('AI will replace me') to opportunity-focused ('AI frees me for higher-value work') by clearly communicating how AI augments rather than replaces human capability.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, generalisability cannot be assessed. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but findings depend heavily on sample composition, organizational context, and AI implementation type.
takeaways: Job crafting behaviors (how employees reshape their roles) shift in response to AI adoption — some employees proactively engage with new tools while others withdraw; understanding which factors drive approach vs. avoidance responses helps design adoption programs that minimize resistance.

Use the approach-avoidance lens when diagnosing AI adoption challenges: employees avoiding AI integration often need reassurance about job security and upskilling support, while those approaching it may benefit from clear role redefinition and skill-building pathways.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis draws on global client work and industry trends, but specific recommendations may reflect practices most applicable to large enterprises in developed economies.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a technical training program — this shifts accountability from HR to business leaders and embeds learning into strategic transformation.

Design upskilling interventions that address mindset shifts and resistance alongside skill gaps, since adoption barriers are often psychological (fear, scepticism) rather than purely capability-based.

Establish clear connections between AI learning goals and business outcomes employees care about — this increases engagement and persistence in behaviour change compared to generic 'future-proofing' messaging.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news report summarizing research findings without detail on original study design, sample size, or geographic scope. The sensationalised headline suggests simplified presentation of complex neuroscience.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies can reveal structural or functional differences in people with psychopathic traits, but these differences don't determine behaviour or explain psychology as simply as headlines suggest.

The word 'shocking' in the title is a red flag for oversimplification — neuroscience findings are often more nuanced than popular media portrays, and correlation between brain differences and personality traits doesn't equal causation.

It's a fun reminder that our brains are genuinely weird and varied in ways we don't fully understand yet, but beware: sensationalised neuroscience claims are rife, and the real science is usually messier and less dramatic than clickbait suggests.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — sample size, geographic scope, and methodology not provided. Findings may be limited to English-language wine reviews or specific wine review platforms.
takeaways: Wine preferences and review language reveal measurable personality patterns — suggesting our taste choices are a window into who we are, not just what we like.
AI can detect psychological traits from seemingly trivial writing (like wine tasting notes), raising interesting questions about how much our everyday language betrays our personality.
A fun reminder that data scientists are finding personality signals in the most unexpected places — your wine review might say more about you than you think.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline framing suggests a single study finding, but without access to the full article, the actual sample size, geographic scope, and methodological strength cannot be assessed.
takeaways: An unexpected biological connection: thyroid hormone levels may influence personality expression, suggesting that some traits we typically think of as purely psychological could have a metabolic component.

The finding is counterintuitive because hyperthyroidism (associated with high energy and anxiety) wouldn't obviously predict 'dark' personality traits — making it a genuinely surprising result that challenges assumptions about personality origins.
Raises a fun 'nature or nurture' twist: if excess thyroid hormone correlates with darker traits, it hints that personality variation might partly stem from biological variation we rarely think about.

articles.title: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Gender Differences in Personality across the Ten Aspects of the Big Five  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet provided. Caution warranted without knowing participant demographics, geographic scope, and cultural context.
takeaways: Personality differences between genders show up across finer-grained personality dimensions, not just the broad Big Five categories — suggesting gender and personality have a more nuanced relationship than pop psychology often suggests.

The 'Ten Aspects' framework reveals variation that the standard Five Factor model might obscure, making this interesting for anyone curious about whether personality science keeps discovering new layers to human differences.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the sample characteristics (likely Western, educated population) and twin study methodology limitations; results may not transfer across different cultural or political contexts.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest authoritarianism has a genetic component, challenging the assumption that political beliefs are purely shaped by environment or upbringing.
The finding that genetic factors influence authoritarian tendencies is counterintuitive — it suggests personality predispositions, not just ideology or messaging, drive some political worldviews.

This research highlights how nature-vs-nurture debates in politics are more nuanced than popular discourse suggests, making it interesting for anyone curious about where our political instincts actually come from.

articles.title: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age - Nature
articles.snippet: Curiosity and surprise differentially affect memory depending on age  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings likely apply across age groups, but generalisability depends on sample composition (size, demographics, cultural background) not evident from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Curiosity and surprise don't work the same memory trick for everyone — age changes how these emotional states help us remember things, which is counterintuitive since we often assume memory boosters work universally.

This challenges the common assumption that 'being curious' or 'being surprised' are universal memory enhancers; the mechanism appears to be age-dependent, making it a neat window into how cognition changes across the lifespan.

The finding is interesting because it suggests that what makes something memorable for a 25-year-old might differ from what makes it stick for a 65-year-old — relevant for anyone curious about how learning strategies might need to shift with age.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad — large global sample across multiple countries and sectors, though representativeness depends on PwC's sampling methodology which is not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Identify which specific workforce fears (e.g., job security, AI displacement, work conditions) are most prevalent in your organisation by comparing PwC's global findings to your own employee survey data — this highlights gaps where psychological safety interventions are most needed.

Use PwC's global benchmarks on workforce hopes and fears to contextualise your own cultural assessment and prioritise which safety concerns (psychological, job security, career development) should be addressed first in your leadership communication and policy design.
Track how employee hopes and fears shift year-on-year using PwC's 2025 baseline — sustained improvements in psychological safety metrics should correlate with changes in these sentiment indicators.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone; findings depend on sample composition (sector, geography, organisational size). The causal pathway (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) requires replication across different contexts to establish robustness.
takeaways: Psychological safety acts as a critical buffer against negative mental health outcomes during AI adoption; prioritise transparent communication and inclusive decision-making processes when introducing AI to reduce employee anxiety and depression risk.

Ethical leadership is essential during AI transitions — leaders must explicitly address ethical concerns, demonstrate commitment to employee wellbeing, and involve staff in AI implementation decisions to maintain trust and psychological safety.

Monitor employee mental health proactively during AI adoption initiatives, particularly among staff who feel excluded from the change process or uncertain about AI's impact on their roles, as depression risk appears elevated when safety and ethical leadership are absent.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws on consulting engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic focus are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create structured opportunities for quieter or marginalised employees to contribute ideas without fear of negative consequences—psychological safety directly enables more inclusive participation and reduces the advantage of those comfortable speaking up.

Leaders should model vulnerability and explicitly solicit dissenting views in team settings; organisations that normalise challenging ideas without fear of retaliation see broader engagement and better decision-making from their full workforce.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full geographic scope, sample size, and methodology not apparent. Frontiers articles vary widely in generalisability; requires access to full paper to assess.
takeaways: Psychological capital (confidence, hope, resilience, optimism) appears to be a key factor enabling employees to view AI as a supportive tool rather than a threat — consider assessing and developing these capacities in your team as you introduce AI systems.

Innovation in AI-driven environments may depend less on technical skills alone and more on employees' psychological readiness and adaptive mindset — factor this into your change management and capability development strategy.
Framing AI as a 'job resource' rather than a replacement threat may unlock both psychological safety and innovation — review how AI is currently positioned in internal communications and training.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings — while psychological safety principles are universal, this report reflects American workplace conditions, labour market dynamics, and organisational practices that may differ significantly from Australian contexts.
takeaways: Identify specific workplace conditions that undermine psychological safety in your team (e.g., fear of speaking up, blame culture) and design targeted interventions to address the root causes rather than symptoms.

Use psychological safety as a lens to evaluate how workplace changes (remote work, restructuring, new technologies) affect employee willingness to take interpersonal risks—this is a leading indicator of engagement and retention.

Assess whether your organisation's feedback and error-handling processes actively build or erode psychological safety; even well-intentioned policies can backfire if employees perceive inconsistent or punitive responses.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and regions, but lacks peer-reviewed validation and may reflect practices among large, well-resourced organisations.
takeaways: Design AI implementations that enhance employee autonomy and decision-making rather than automating them away — frame AI as a capability enabler to build psychological safety around new tools.

Create clear governance structures and transparent communication about how AI will be deployed and what employee roles will change, reducing uncertainty-driven anxiety that undermines psychological safety.
Invest in upskilling programmes that help employees feel capable and in control when working alongside AI, moving beyond basic literacy to meaningful competence that boosts confidence and trust.
